answer.label: Adapted from a play by
answer.sourceLine: This is a compressed version of dialogue in Wilde’s An Ideal Husband, Act IV. Lord Goring supplies the longer contrast between women’s emotions and men’s intellect; it is dramatic dialogue, not a documented personal pronouncement by Joyce.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Lord Goring; the contrast is subsequently repeated by Lady Chiltern
The popular sentence compresses two sentences of dialogue

source.excerpt: A woman’s life revolves in curves of emotions. It is upon lines of intellect that a man’s life progresses.
trail: The primary play ↗ identifies the speaker and shows the longer contrast within his advice to Lady Chiltern.
Wikiquote’s Joyce entry ↗ marks the compressed form as misattributed and directs readers to Wilde.
source.rightsNote: Wilde’s underlying English dialogue is public domain; the date and maker of the popular compression have not been established. The source excerpt reproduces the old play, while the headline identifies the circulating variant.

author.bio: Oscar Wilde wrote social comedies, fiction and criticism, combining theatrical wit with criticism of respectable public appearances. An Ideal Husband places a politician’s concealed wrongdoing inside the expectations of marriage and public life.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Lord Goring wants Lady Chiltern to forgive her husband and preserve his political career. His appeal rests on a conspicuously unequal account of men’s ambitions and women’s marital duties; the surrounding dialogue matters when interpreting its claim.
The line is later echoed by Lady Chiltern as she accepts that advice. Pulling a compressed form out as a free-standing maxim obscures both its dramatic speaker and its place in the plot.
